kurals.tamil:
மிகினும் குறையினும் நோய்செய்யும் நூலோர்
வளிமுதலா எண்ணிய மூன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Miginum kuraiyinum noiseyyum noolor
valimudhalaa enniya moondru.
kurals.meaning: The three bodily forces that medical authors count, beginning with wind, cause disease whether they grow too strong or fall too low.
kurals.elementary: Think of a bicycle tyre: pump in too much air and it bursts, let out too much and it goes flat. Valluvar says the body has three such forces inside it, and it stays healthy only when each one is just right.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with theory before practice: noolor (நூலோர், 'the authors of the treatises') are the medical writers, and vali mudhalaa enniya moondru (வளிமுதலா எண்ணிய மூன்று, 'the three reckoned with wind first') are the three humours that Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss as vaatham, piththam and silethumam (வாதம், பித்தம், சிலேத்துமம்), i.e. the vata-pitta-kapha triad of Ayurveda and Siddha medicine. The decisive words are miginum kuraiyinum (மிகினும் குறையினும், 'whether in excess or in deficiency'): illness is defined not as an invading thing but as loss of proportion. Following Parimelazhagar, Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan add that the humours are disturbed through a person's food and activity (உணவும் செயல்களும்), which is why the following couplets turn at once to eating. The chapter closes the Natpiyal section of Porutpaal in the traditional arrangement, a placement commentators explain by treating bodily health as the last of the things a ruler and householder must secure. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Charaka Samhita defines disease as disequilibrium of the body's constituents and health as their equilibrium, and treats vata, pitta and kapha as the doshas whose increase or decrease produces illness.
hinduism.explanation: Classical Ayurveda makes balance the very definition of health and imbalance, in either direction, the definition of disease.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the medical theory the Kural's noolor are summarising: the three humours harm by being too much or too little.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Doctrinally a near one-to-one match and almost certainly the tradition Valluvar has in view; wording paraphrased because no translation could be checked live this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: Ecclesiastes counsels against being righteous overmuch or wicked overmuch, urging the one who fears God to avoid both extremes.
christianity.explanation: The Preacher warns that going too far in either direction destroys a person.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats harm as coming from both excess and its opposite, though the subject is conduct rather than the body.
christianity._accuracy_note: Next-best match: shares the two-sided logic of excess and defect but has nothing to say about bodily humours or medicine.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the heaven He raised and imposed the balance That you not transgress within the balance. And establish weight in justice and do not make deficient the balance.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents creation as resting on a divinely set balance that must be neither exceeded nor made deficient.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's rule for the body's three humours mirrors this cosmic warning against both transgressing and short-weighting the balance.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the balance-against-excess-and-deficiency structure matches, but the verse concerns cosmic and commercial justice, not health.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Since maintaining a healthy and sound body is among the ways of God - for one cannot understand or have any knowledge of the Creator, if he is ill - therefore, he must avoid that which harms the body and accustom himself to that which is healthful and helps the body become stronger.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides, himself a physician, opens his health code by making bodily soundness a religious duty and framing medicine as avoiding what harms and cultivating what strengthens.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts begin a treatment of health with the principle that the body must be kept from what disturbs it.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:1 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a fitting chapter-opening parallel, but it lacks the Kural's specific theory of three humours in excess or deficiency.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha reminds the over-strenuous monk Sona that a lute sounds well only when its strings are neither too tight nor too slack, and tells him to tune his effort the same way.
buddhism.explanation: The simile teaches that both overstrain and slackness spoil the result; balance is what makes the instrument play.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural applies the same neither-too-much-nor-too-little rule to the body's three humours.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of a well-known sutta, not checked live; strong structural parallel, but about meditative effort, not physical health.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Vêdanîya is twofold, pleasure and pain; there are many subdivisions of pleasure and so there are of pain also.”
jainism.explanation: In Jain doctrine the experience of bodily pain and pleasure is the fruition of vedaniya karma, one of the eight kinds of karmic matter binding the soul.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural traces disease to an imbalance of three humours, Jainism traces the felt pain of disease further back, to karma, a different causal account of the same suffering.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; included as an honest contrast, since canonical Jain scripture offers no humoral theory of disease.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus warns Icarus to fly a middle course, neither so low that the sea's damp weighs down his wings nor so high that the sun's heat melts their wax; Icarus soars too high and falls.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes both extremes deadly and only the middle path safe.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that harm comes from too much and from too little alike.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not verified live; the excess-and-defect structure is a good fit, but the subject is flight, not the body.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Timaeus, Plato explains that the body is compacted of four elements, and that the unnatural excess or defect of these, or their shifting out of their proper place, is the origin of disorders and diseases.
philosophy.explanation: Plato gives a Greek version of humoral pathology in which disease is the excess or deficiency of the body's constituents.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's thesis, with four elements in place of three humours.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one in doctrine; paraphrased because the Jowett wording was not checked live this session.

kurals.tamil:
மருந்தென வேண்டாவாம் யாக்கைக்கு அருந்தியது
அற்றது போற்றி உணின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Marundhena vendaavaam yaakkaikku arundhiyadhu
atradhu potri unin.
kurals.meaning: The body needs nothing called medicine if a person eats only after making sure that what was eaten before has been fully digested.
kurals.elementary: You would not pour more water into a glass that is still full; it would spill everywhere. Valluvar says the stomach is like that glass: wait until it has finished the last meal before you fill it again, and you will hardly ever need a doctor.
kurals.university: The couplet makes a bold claim, that medicine (marundhu, மருந்து) becomes unnecessary (vendaavaam, வேண்டாவாம்) for the body (yaakkai, யாக்கை), on one condition: arundhiyadhu atradhu potri unin (அருந்தியது அற்றது போற்றி உணின்), 'if one eats after carefully confirming that what was taken has been digested'. Atradhu (அற்றது, literally 'that which has ceased') is the technical verb for complete digestion that recurs in 943 and 944. Potri (போற்றி) means not 'praising' here but 'observing with care'; Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as examining the state of digestion, and Kalaignar as allowing the proper interval between meals. Parimelazhagar's tradition reads the hyperbole as a statement of priority: prevention through regimen ranks above cure. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Among Charaka's rules for eating is that one should eat only after the previous meal has been digested, since food taken on top of undigested food disturbs all the doshas.
hinduism.explanation: Ayurvedic dietetics makes the digestion of the last meal the precondition for the next.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's rule almost word for word: eat only when what you ate before has been digested.
hinduism.source: Charaka Samhita, Vimanasthana 1.24 (rules of eating), paraphrase
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close doctrinal match; paraphrased because the translation was not verified live, and the exact verse number should be checked.

christianity.quote_or_event: Jesus answers his critics that those who are healthy have no need of a physician, only those who are sick.
christianity.explanation: The saying assumes the plain truth that a sound body does not need the doctor.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural tells how to stay among the healthy who need no medicine.
christianity._accuracy_note: Next-best match: shares the healthy-need-no-physician premise, but Jesus uses it as a metaphor for sinners and says nothing about diet.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that there are two blessings in which many people are cheated: health and free time.
islam.explanation: The hadith counts health among God's greatest gifts and warns that people squander it.
islam.tie_back: The Kural shows the simple discipline that guards this gift so that medicine is never needed.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not checked live this session; it values health but gives no rule about eating after digestion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Whoever conducts himself in the ways which we have drawn up, I will guarantee that he will not become ill throughout his life, until he reaches advanced age and dies. He will not need a doctor.”
judaism.explanation: After setting out rules of eating, exercise and rest, Maimonides promises that anyone who follows them will never need a physician.
judaism.tie_back: Maimonides makes the Kural's exact promise: right regimen at meals means no need for medicine.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:20 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; the 'no need of a doctor' guarantee is a near one-to-one match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada names good health as the highest gain and contentment as the greatest wealth.
buddhism.explanation: Among all the things a person can acquire, the verse ranks freedom from illness first.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows how that highest gain is kept: by eating only when the last meal is gone.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified live; it praises health but supplies no dietary rule.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The mind of those who always live in unfrequented lodgings, who eat low food, and who subdue their senses, will not be attacked by the foe, Love, who is vanquished as disease is by medicine.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana treats plain, restrained eating as itself a remedy that keeps the passions from attacking the monk.
jainism.tie_back: As the Kural makes careful eating stand in for medicine for the body, the Jain text makes restrained eating serve as medicine for the soul.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the food-as-medicine idea is shared, but the Jain aim is spiritual purity rather than bodily health.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that before Pandora opened her jar, the races of men lived on earth free from ills, from hard toil and from the heavy sicknesses that bring death.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth imagines an original human life in which sickness, and so medicine, did not exist.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural holds out a modest version of that sickness-free life, earned by a habit of eating rather than lost by a jar.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 90-92 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White), paraphrase
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best match: shares the picture of life without need for cure, but the myth blames fate, not diet.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates in the Republic scorns the need for medicine that arises not from wounds or epidemics but from idleness and a self-indulgent way of living that fills the body with fluxes and winds.
philosophy.explanation: Plato argues that most need for doctors is self-inflicted by bad habits of life.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural draws the positive conclusion: right habits of eating remove the need for medicine.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic III, 405c-d (tr. Benjamin Jowett), paraphrase
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on lifestyle making medicine necessary; paraphrased because the passage was not checked live.

kurals.tamil:
அற்றால் அறவறிந்து உண்க அஃதுடம்பு
பெற்றான் நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Atraal aravarindhu unga ahdhudambu
petraan nedidhuykkum aaru.
kurals.meaning: Once the previous meal is digested, eat knowing the right measure; that is how one who has received a body keeps it going for a long time.
kurals.elementary: A car runs far if you fill the tank properly and do not overflow it. Valluvar says your body is a gift you have been given, and eating the right amount at the right time is how you make it last a long, long time.
kurals.university: Atraal (அற்றால், 'when it has been digested') picks up the condition of 942, and adds aravarindhu (அறவறிந்து, அற + அறிந்து): Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read it as knowing the needed quantity, Puliyur Kesikan simply as eating in measure. The second line names the payoff: udambu petraan (உடம்பு பெற்றான், 'he who has obtained a body') can nedidhu uykkum (நெடிது உய்க்கும், 'carry it on long'). Kesikan glosses the body as 'this human frame so hard to obtain' (பெறுவதற்கரியதான இந்த மானிட யாக்கை), an Indian commonplace that human birth is rare and should not be wasted through gluttony. Parimelazhagar's line of interpretation thus links diet to longevity, not merely to comfort. Some editions print the first line as அற்றால் அளவறிந்து; ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net both read அறவறிந்து.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who is temperate in his habits of eating, sleeping, working and recreation can mitigate all material pains by practicing the yoga system.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that regulated eating (yuktahara), along with regulated sleep and work, is the ground of a pain-free yogic life.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's 'eat knowing the measure' is the Gita's yuktahara, here tied to long life rather than to yoga.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.17 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, As It Is, 1972)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; strong fit on measured eating, though the Gita's goal is yoga rather than longevity.

christianity.quote_or_event: “By surfeiting have many perished; but he that taketh heed prolongeth his life.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira warns that overeating has killed many, while the one who is careful about food lengthens his days.
christianity.tie_back: It is a near paraphrase of the Kural: measured eating is the way to keep the body long.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; near one-to-one, linking careful eating directly to longer life.

islam.quote_or_event: “O children of Adam, take your adornment [i.e., wear your clothing] at every masjid, and eat and drink, but be not excessive. Indeed, He likes not those who commit excess.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an permits eating and drinking but forbids going beyond measure.
islam.tie_back: Both texts allow food freely while insisting that its measure be known and kept.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong fit on measure in eating, though it does not mention digestion or longevity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “One should not eat until his stomach is full. Rather, [he should stop when] he has eaten to close to three quarter's of full satisfaction.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides gives a concrete measure: stop eating at about three quarters of fullness.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'knowing the measure', given an actual number.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:2 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong match on measure, though longevity is promised elsewhere in the chapter (4:20).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When a man is always mindful, knowing moderation in eating, his discomfort fades, and he ages slowly, taking care of his life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha spoke this verse to King Pasenadi, who was panting after eating rice by the bucketful; the king had it recited at every meal and slimmed down.
buddhism.tie_back: Knowing the measure in eating so that one 'ages slowly, taking care of his life' is the Kural's promise of long life almost exactly.
buddhism.source: Donapaka Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 3.13 (tr. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on SuttaCentral; a near one-to-one match on measure in eating and prolonged life.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who takes less food than he usually does, in the extreme case but one mouthful, performs abstinence with regard to substance.”
jainism.explanation: Avamodarika, eating less than one's full measure, is one of the six external austerities in Jain discipline.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism, like the Kural, makes the measure of food a matter of deliberate knowledge, though it sets the measure below fullness to burn off karma rather than to prolong life.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; shares measured eating, but its purpose is ascetic, not health or longevity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The maxim 'Nothing in excess' (meden agan) was inscribed at Apollo's temple at Delphi, which Plato says the sages dedicated as the first fruits of their wisdom.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Delphic god's own precinct carried a warning against excess in all things.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural applies the Delphic rule to the dinner plate.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked live; a general maxim of moderation with no specific reference to food or long life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...both excessive and defective exercise destroys the strength, and similarly drink or food which is above or below a certain amount destroys the health, while that which is proportionate both produces and increases and preserves it.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle uses diet as his model for the mean: the right amount of food produces, increases and preserves health.
philosophy.tie_back: Proportionate food that 'preserves' health is the Kural's measured eating that keeps the body long.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.2 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive; close match on measured food preserving health.

kurals.tamil:
அற்றது அறிந்து கடைப்பிடித்து மாறல்ல
துய்க்க துவரப் பசித்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Atradhu arindhu kadaippidiththu maaralla
thuykka thuvarap pasiththu.
kurals.meaning: Knowing that the earlier meal is digested, keep firmly to foods that agree with the body, and eat them only when truly hungry.
kurals.elementary: A plant needs water, but only when its soil has dried, and only clean water, not juice or soda. Valluvar says eat when you are really hungry, and choose the food that suits your body.
kurals.university: The couplet adds two refinements to the rule of digestion. Maaralla (மாறல்ல, 'things that are not contrary') are foods that do not disagree with one's constitution; Pappaiah extends this to foods unsuited to the body and to the season (உடம்பிற்கும் காலத்திற்கும் ஒவ்வாத). Kadaippidiththu (கடைப்பிடித்து) means holding firmly to such foods as a fixed practice. Thuvarap pasiththu (துவரப் பசித்து), 'being thoroughly hungry', makes real hunger, not appetite or habit, the signal to eat. Pope's translation renders the sense as 'when hunger prompteth thee, with constant care, the viands choose that well agree'. The idea of wholesome and unwholesome food relative to the person (Sanskrit satmya) is shared with Ayurveda, and the Parimelazhagar tradition reads the couplet as practical dietetics. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Foods in the mode of goodness increase the duration of life, purify one's existence and give strength, health, happiness and satisfaction. Such nourishing foods are sweet, juicy, fattening and palatable.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita classes foods by their effect, praising those that are agreeable and promote life, strength and health.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's 'foods that agree with the body' correspond to the Gita's sattvic foods.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.8 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, As It Is, 1972)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; matches choosing agreeable food, but says nothing of waiting for hunger or digestion.

christianity.quote_or_event: The Preacher calls a land blessed whose princes eat in due season, for strength and not for drunkenness.
christianity.explanation: Ecclesiastes praises rulers who eat at the proper time and for the right purpose.
christianity.tie_back: Eating in due season for strength parallels the Kural's eating only at true hunger.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified live; shares the idea of eating at the right time, but is a political rather than medical remark.

islam.quote_or_event: God tells the Children of Israel to eat of the good things He has provided and not to transgress therein.
islam.explanation: The Qur'an pairs eating what is good with a warning against going beyond bounds.
islam.tie_back: Both texts call for wholesome food taken within limits.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked live; fits wholesome food with restraint, but not the Kural's rules on hunger and digestion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They are as follows: a person should never eat unless he is hungry, nor drink unless thirsty.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides' first practical rule of health is to eat only from real hunger.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'eat when thoroughly hungry' stated as law.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:1 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; near one-to-one on the hunger rule; the choice of agreeable foods is treated in 4:7-11.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches monks to reflect wisely when they take almsfood: not for fun, intoxication or beautification, but only to sustain the body, to end the discomfort of hunger and to support the spiritual life.
buddhism.explanation: The daily reflection on food makes the relief of hunger and the support of the body the only proper reasons for eating.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes real hunger, not pleasure, the occasion for eating.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a standard formula, not verified live; good fit on eating for need, but the goal is spiritual, not medical.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A Sramana engaged in austerities, who longs for righteousness, should eat the proper quantity of allowed food, should select a companion of right understanding, and should live in a place suited to seclusion.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain monk is to eat only permitted food, and only in the proper quantity.
jainism.tie_back: Choosing allowed food in proper quantity echoes the Kural's choosing agreeable food at the right time, with the Jain criterion being ahimsa and discipline rather than bodily constitution.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; partial fit, since 'allowed' means ritually and ethically permitted, not medically suited.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Alcinous' palace the grieving Odysseus says there is nothing more shameless than the belly, which commands a man to eat even in his deepest sorrow.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's hero admits that hunger rules even a hero's heart.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural accepts hunger's claim but tames it: eat only when hunger is real, and eat what suits you.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best match, paraphrased: about hunger's insistence, not about choosing wholesome food or waiting for digestion.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Xenophon reports that Socrates ate only as much as he could eat with relish, and came to his meals so ready that the appetite itself was his sauce.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates let genuine hunger, not rich dishes, make food pleasant.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's rule to eat when thoroughly hungry, lived out by a philosopher.
philosophy.source: Xenophon, Memorabilia I.3.5 (tr. E. C. Marchant), paraphrase
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit; paraphrased because the translation was not checked live.

kurals.tamil:
மாறுபாடு இல்லாத உண்டி மறுத்துண்ணின்
ஊறுபாடு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Maarupaadu illaadha undi maruththunnin
oorupaadu illai uyirkku.
kurals.meaning: If one eats wholesome food and still holds back from eating too much of it, no harm comes to one's life.
kurals.elementary: Even your favourite ice cream will give you a tummy ache if you eat the whole tub. Valluvar says that even good food must be eaten with a 'no, that's enough' at the right moment.
kurals.university: Maarupaadu illaadha undi (மாறுபாடு இல்லாத உண்டி) is food that does not clash with the body, the same category as maaralla in 944. The key word is maruththu (மறுத்து, 'refusing'): Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as refusing more once the measure is reached, and Kesikan as eating not as the mind desires but only as much as causes no illness. Solomon Pappaiah takes a different line, reading maruththu as rejecting unsuitable foods, so that the couplet becomes about selection rather than quantity; this is a genuine interpretive divergence. Oorupaadu (ஊறுபாடு) is injury or harm, and uyirkku (உயிர்க்கு) 'to life' or 'to the soul dwelling in the body'. Parimelazhagar's reading, followed by most modern commentators, stresses restraint even with good food. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Foods that are too bitter, too sour, salty, pungent, dry and hot, are liked by people in the modes of passion. Such foods cause pain, distress, and disease.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita warns that foods chosen for intense taste rather than wholesomeness bring disease.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's 'food without contrariety' is the opposite of these disease-causing rajasic foods.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.9 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, As It Is, 1972)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; addresses harmful kinds of food, not the restraint in quantity that is the Kural's main point.

christianity.quote_or_event: Proverbs advises that if you find honey you should eat only as much as is sufficient for you, lest you be filled with it and vomit it.
christianity.explanation: Even the sweetest good thing must be taken only up to sufficiency.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's lesson that even agreeable food must be eaten with refusal of excess.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong fit on restraint with good food; paraphrased because the verse was not checked live this session.

islam.quote_or_event: “The human does not fill any container that is worse than his stomach. It is sufficient for the son of Adam to eat what will support his back. If this is not possible, then a third for food, a third for drink, and third for his breath.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet sets the limit of eating at what keeps one upright, or at most a third of the stomach for food.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hadith asks for deliberate restraint even with lawful, wholesome food.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; close match on refusing excess even of good food.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A man who is wise, overcomes his desires, is not drawn by his appetites and eats nothing of the aforementioned unless he needs them for a medical reason, is [indeed] heroic.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides calls the one who masters his appetite at table a hero.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's maruththu, refusing at the table, is exactly this heroic self-mastery.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:10 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong fit on restraint, though it concerns avoiding mildly harmful foods rather than limiting good ones.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares right eating to parents crossing a desert who must eat the flesh of their dead child to survive: they eat only to get across, without any relish or excess.
buddhism.explanation: The stark simile teaches that food should be taken only for sustenance, never for indulgence.
buddhism.tie_back: It pushes to an extreme the Kural's counsel to eat even good food with refusal of excess.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified live; shares restraint in eating but is aimed at non-attachment, not health.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Abstention from dainty food means abstention from such highly nourishing food and drink as milk, curds, ghee, &c.”
jainism.explanation: Rasaparityaga, giving up rich and tasty foods, is one of the six external Jain austerities.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism, like the Kural, asks the eater to refuse what appetite wants, though it renounces even wholesome rich foods for the soul's sake.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; partial fit, since the Jain aim is ascetic purification rather than freedom from illness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Stranded on Thrinacia, Odysseus' starving companions slaughter the forbidden cattle of the Sun despite his warnings; Zeus destroys their ship, and only Odysseus, who refused the meat, survives.
greek_mythology.explanation: The men who could not refuse food perished, while the one who held back lived.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's promise, that the one who refuses excess suffers no harm to life, is played out in mythic terms.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best match: the food was sacrilegious rather than unhealthy, so the parallel is only to restraint saving life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epicurus writes to Menoeceus that plain fare gives as much pleasure as a costly diet once the pain of want is removed, and that becoming used to simple food is a full supply of health.
philosophy.explanation: The philosopher of pleasure himself argues that restraint and simple food are the true road to health and lasting pleasure.
philosophy.tie_back: This supports the Kural's claim that wholesome food eaten with restraint keeps life free from harm.
philosophy.source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus (Diogenes Laertius X.130-131, tr. R. D. Hicks), paraphrase
philosophy._accuracy_note: Reasonable thematic fit; paraphrased because the Hicks translation was not checked live.

kurals.tamil:
இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்கண் இன்பம்போல் நிற்கும்
கழிபேர் இரையான்கண் நோய்.
kurals.transliteration:
Izhivarindhu unbaankan inbampol nirkum
kazhiper iraiyaankan noi.
kurals.meaning: Just as well-being stays with the one who knows to eat a little less, so disease stays with the one who devours far too much.
kurals.elementary: Two friends go to a party. One eats until he is nicely full and goes home happy. The other stuffs himself and spends the night with a stomach ache. Valluvar says that is how it goes every time.
kurals.university: The couplet is a balanced antithesis. Izhivu (இழிவு) here means 'lessness': Varadarasanar glosses izhivarindhu unbaan as one who knows what the lesser measure is, and Kesikan as one who eats a little below the full measure; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it more morally as one who knows that taking more than needed is base, exploiting the word's other sense of 'meanness'. Inbam (இன்பம்) is well-being or pleasure, which nirkum (நிற்கும், 'stays, abides'). Kazhiper iraiyaan (கழிபேர் இரையான்) is a striking phrase: irai (இரை) is the word for an animal's prey or fodder, so the glutton is pictured as a beast gulping feed, and kazhiper (கழிபேர்) intensifies it to 'exceedingly great'. Disease abides with him as surely as health with the moderate eater. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There is no possibility of one's becoming a yogī, O Arjuna, if one eats too much, or eats too little, sleeps too much or does not sleep enough.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna makes moderation in eating a precondition of the disciplined, well-ordered life.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita treats the over-eater as one who has forfeited the good state that the moderate keep.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.16 (tr. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, As It Is, 1972)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on asitis.com; good fit on moderation, though the stake is yogic attainment rather than disease.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Sound sleep cometh of moderate eating: he riseth early, and his wits are with him: but the pain of watching, and choler, and pangs of the belly, are with an unsatiable man.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira sets the rested, clear-headed moderate eater against the sleepless, bilious, cramped glutton.
christianity.tie_back: It is the same two-sided picture as the Kural: well-being stays with the moderate and suffering with the insatiable.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a near one-to-one antithesis, even down to the glutton's bodily pains.

islam.quote_or_event: “A believer eats in one intestine (is satisfied with a little food), and a kafir (unbeliever) eats in seven intestines (eats much food).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet contrasts the believer, content with little, with one who eats voraciously.
islam.tie_back: The Kural draws the same contrast between the one who eats little and the one who devours, measured by health rather than faith.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; the contrast of little and much matches, but the hadith's stake is spiritual character, not illness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As long as one exercises, exerts himself greatly, does not eat to the point of satiation and has loose bowels, he will not suffer sickness and he will grow in strength.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides promises freedom from sickness and growing strength to one who stops short of satiety.
judaism.tie_back: Eating short of fullness and keeping well is the first half of the Kural's antithesis.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:14 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong fit, with the glutton's fate given in the next halakha (used for 947).

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that Mara overthrows one who lives fixed on pleasant things, with senses unguarded and immoderate in eating, as wind topples a weak tree, but cannot shake one who is moderate in eating and restrained, as wind cannot shake a rocky mountain.
buddhism.explanation: The paired verses set the immoderate eater, easily overthrown, against the moderate one who stands firm.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's twin portrait of the moderate eater and the glutton has the same two-sided form.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified live; matching antithesis, though the danger is Mara rather than disease.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant food should not be enjoyed with preference, for it generally makes men over-strong; and desires rush upon the strong, like birds upon a tree with sweet fruits.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana warns that rich eating breeds an excess that attracts the passions as fruit attracts birds.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural sees disease settling on the glutton, the Jain text sees desires swarming on him.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; parallel structure of overeating inviting harm, but the harm is passion, not illness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Homer introduces the beggar Irus as notorious for his insatiable belly, always eating and drinking, big to look at but with no strength or force in him; Odysseus fells him with a single blow.
greek_mythology.explanation: The glutton's bulk hides weakness, and he is easily brought down.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Irus embodies the Kural's kazhiper iraiyaan, the over-eater with whom weakness abides.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best match, paraphrased: Irus's weakness is not presented as disease, and there is no moderate counterpart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca observes that simple food once kept people healthy, and that the multiplying of rich dishes has multiplied diseases, so that one who wonders at the countless diseases should count the cooks.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic ties the growth of disease directly to luxurious overeating.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's cooks and diseases are the Kural's glutton with whom illness stays.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 95.15-23 (tr. R. M. Gummere), paraphrase
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit; paraphrased because the Gummere wording was not checked live.

kurals.tamil:
தீயள வன்றித் தெரியான் பெரிதுண்ணின்
நோயள வின்றிப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Theeyala vandrith theriyaan peridhunnin
noyala vindrip padum.
kurals.meaning: One who thoughtlessly eats a great deal, beyond the measure of the digestive fire, will suffer diseases beyond measure.
kurals.elementary: A small campfire can cook a small pot. If you pile a whole tree on it, the fire chokes and smoke goes everywhere. Valluvar says your tummy has a little fire too, and if you overload it, troubles pile up.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a wordplay of measure: thee alavu (தீ அளவு, 'the measure of the fire') against noi alavu indri (நோய் அளவின்றி, 'diseases without measure'). The fire is the pasi-thee (பசித்தீ), the 'fire of hunger' or digestive fire, as Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss it; it corresponds to the Ayurvedic jatharagni, whose strength determines how much food can be digested. Theriyaan (தெரியான்) is 'one who does not discern', and Kesikan adds that he ignores both the time and the quantity. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads thee alavu instead as an analogy to one who does not know how to use fire in measure, a minority reading. Parimelazhagar's tradition takes the metaphor medically, so that the couplet states a law: exceed the fire's measure and illness exceeds all measure. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Charaka teaches that one should eat in proper measure, and that the right quantity of food depends on the strength of the digestive fire (agni).
hinduism.explanation: In Ayurveda the digestive fire sets the limit of how much food can be taken without harm.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's thee alavu, the measure of the fire, stated as medical doctrine.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one doctrinal match on agni governing quantity; paraphrased because no translation was checked live.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For excess of meats bringeth sickness, and surfeiting will turn into choler.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira states plainly that eating too much produces sickness and biliousness.
christianity.tie_back: Excess of food bringing sickness is the Kural's rule that eating beyond measure brings disease beyond measure.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; close match on excess causing illness, without the fire image.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur'an describes those who reject faith as enjoying themselves and eating as grazing cattle eat, without thought.
islam.explanation: Thoughtless, animal-like eating is presented as the mark of a heedless life.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's theriyaan, the undiscerning eater, is likewise one who eats without thought of measure.
islam._accuracy_note: Next-best match, paraphrased: concerns heedlessness and faith, not illness from overeating.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Overeating is like poison to anyone's body. It is the main source of all illness. Most illnesses which afflict a man are caused by harmful foods or by his filling his belly and overeating, even of healthful foods.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides traces most human illness to overeating, even of good food.
judaism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's claim that eating beyond measure brings diseases beyond measure.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:15 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; near one-to-one on overeating as the source of many illnesses.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who gets drowsy from overeating, fond of sleep, rolling round the bed like a great hog stuffed with grain: that dullard returns to the womb again and again.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada, traditionally linked to King Pasenadi's overeating, pictures the glutton as a sluggish, stuffed hog.
buddhism.tie_back: The thoughtless over-eater of the Kural is this stuffed, dull figure, though the Buddhist cost is rebirth rather than disease.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on SuttaCentral; vivid on overeating's dullness, but the consequence is rebirth, not illness.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As in a forest, full of fuel, a fire fanned by the wind cannot be extinguished, so the fire (as it were) of the senses of him who eats as he lists; it does not benefit any chaste man.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana uses the image of fire fed with too much fuel for the senses inflamed by unrestrained eating.
jainism.tie_back: Both texts reach for fire to describe eating without measure, the Kural for the digestive fire and the Jain text for the fire of the senses.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; striking shared fire imagery, but the harm is to restraint, not to bodily health.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid tells how Erysichthon, cursed by Ceres with Hunger for felling her sacred oak, eats ever more and craves ever more, as fire never refuses fuel, until he consumes his fortune and at last his own flesh.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth makes boundless eating a self-devouring fire that destroys the eater.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Erysichthon is the extreme of the Kural's man who eats beyond the fire's measure and suffers without measure.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit with shared fire imagery; paraphrased because the translation was not checked live.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Growing bodies have the most innate heat; they therefore require the most food, for otherwise their bodies are wasted. In old persons the heat is feeble, and therefore they require little fuel, as it were, to the flame, for it would be extinguished by much.”
philosophy.explanation: Hippocrates measures how much food a body needs by its inner heat, and warns that too much fuel smothers a weak flame.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's thee alavu exactly: food must match the measure of the body's fire.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive; a near one-to-one match on food measured against inner fire.

kurals.tamil:
நோய்நாடி நோய்முதல் நாடி அதுதணிக்கும்
வாய்நாடி வாய்ப்பச் செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Noinaadi noimudhal naadi adhuthanikkum
vaainaadi vaaippach cheyal.
kurals.meaning: Find out what the disease is, find out its cause, find out the way to relieve it, and then act in the way that fits.
kurals.elementary: When your bike makes a funny noise, a good mechanic first finds which part is wrong, then why it broke, then how to fix it, and only then gets out the tools. Valluvar says a good doctor does the same with a sick person.
kurals.university: The most quoted couplet of the chapter is built on a threefold naadi (நாடி, 'having examined'): the disease (noi), its root or first cause (noi mudhal, நோய் முதல்), and the means (vaai, வாய்) that will abate it (thanikkum, தணிக்கும்). Only then comes vaaippach cheyal (வாய்ப்பச் செயல்), 'act fittingly': Kesikan reads it as treating without error in procedure, Varadarasanar as in a way suited to the body. Commentators note the sequence of diagnosis, aetiology and therapy as a complete clinical method; Kalaignar adds that it applies to the ills of society as well as of the body. The repetition of naadi and of vaai/vaaippa gives the line a deliberate, step-by-step rhythm. The couplet appears in the sung version of the chapter by P. A. Muthukrishnan quoted on thirukkural.net. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Charaka instructs the physician to examine the disease first and only afterwards the medicine, and then to begin treatment with knowledge.
hinduism.explanation: Classical Ayurveda puts diagnosis before any prescription.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's order: know the disease and its cause before choosing the remedy.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close doctrinal match; paraphrased and the verse number given from standard citation, not checked live.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then give place to the physician, for the Lord hath created him: let him not go from thee, for thou hast need of him. There is a time when in their hands there is good success. For they shall also pray unto the Lord, that he would prosper that, which they give for ease and remedy to prolong life.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira honours the physician and describes him seeking the right remedy and the right moment to bring ease.
christianity.tie_back: It supports the Kural's skilled, careful physician, though without its diagnostic method.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; honours medical skill and timing, but has no disease-cause-remedy sequence.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is a remedy for every malady, and when the remedy is applied to the disease it is cured with the permission of Allah, the Exalted and Glorious.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that every disease has its proper remedy, which cures when correctly matched to it.
islam.tie_back: Matching the right remedy to the disease is the Kural's 'find the means that abates it'.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; strong on the disease-remedy match, without explicit diagnosis of cause.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud derives from the words 'and he shall surely heal' that the Torah grants the physician permission to heal, so that medical treatment is a sanctioned and even obligatory act.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic law affirms the physician's work as legitimate rather than an intrusion on God's will.
judaism.tie_back: It provides the religious warrant for the physician the Kural describes, though not his method.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 85a (on Exodus 21:19), paraphrase
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified live; endorses medicine in general but does not describe diagnosis.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Buddhaghosa explains the Four Noble Truths through medicine: suffering is like the disease, its origin like the cause of the disease, its cessation like the cure, and the path like the medicine.
buddhism.explanation: The commentarial tradition reads the Buddha's core teaching as a physician's diagnosis, aetiology, prognosis and prescription.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's sequence of disease, its cause and its remedy, raised to a spiritual method.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong structural match; paraphrased because the Nanamoli translation was not checked live.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Love and hatred are caused by Karman, and they say that Karman has its origin in delusion; Karman is the root of birth and death, and birth and death they call misery. Misery ceases on the absence of delusion, delusion ceases on the absence of desire, desire ceases on the absence of greed, greed ceases on the absence of property.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana traces suffering back through karma and delusion to its roots and shows how removing each root ends it, calling final liberation recovery 'from the long illness'.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's method of finding the disease, then its root cause, then what removes it, applied to the soul's misery.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.7-8, cf. 32.110 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a genuinely Jain causal diagnosis of suffering, applied to spiritual rather than bodily illness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Menelaus is wounded by an arrow, the healer Machaon, son of Asclepius, comes, draws the arrow, looks at the wound, sucks out the blood and skilfully spreads on it the soothing remedies that Chiron had given his father.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's physician examines the wound first and then applies the proper remedy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Machaon follows the Kural's order: look at the injury, then bring the fitting treatment.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit, paraphrased from a well-known scene; an arrow wound needs little diagnosis of hidden cause.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato contrasts the slave doctor who prescribes hastily with the free doctor who examines the disease from its origin and according to nature, questions the patient and his friends, and prescribes only after understanding the case.
philosophy.explanation: Plato's model physician investigates the nature and origin of the illness before he treats.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's physician who examines the disease and its cause before acting.
philosophy.source: Plato, Laws IV, 720a-e (tr. Benjamin Jowett), paraphrase
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit; paraphrased because the passage was not checked live.

kurals.tamil:
உற்றான் அளவும் பிணியளவும் காலமும்
கற்றான் கருதிச் செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Utraan alavum piniyalavum kaalamum
katraan karudhich cheyal.
kurals.meaning: The learned physician should act only after weighing the patient's condition, the extent of the disease, and the time or season.
kurals.elementary: A baby and a grown-up with the same cold do not get the same dose of medicine. Valluvar says a good doctor thinks about who is sick, how sick they are, and what time it is before deciding what to do.
kurals.university: Three measures must be weighed: utraan alavu (உற்றான் அளவு), the measure of the one afflicted, which Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss as age and the like, and Kesikan as the patient's strength; pini alavu (பிணியளவு), the extent and nature of the disease; and kaalam (காலம்), which Sivayogi Sivakumar reads as the climate of the season, Kalaignar as the right time for treatment, and Pappaiah as both the duration of the illness and the time needed to cure it. The agent is katraan (கற்றான்), 'the one who has learned', i.e. the physician trained in the medical texts, and karudhi (கருதி) means 'having deliberated'. The couplet thus individualises treatment, echoing Ayurveda's attention to the patient's constitution and to season (ritu). Pope renders it 'the habitudes of patient and disease, the crises of the ill these must the learned leech think over well'. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Charaka lays down a tenfold examination of the patient, including his constitution, strength, body measure, power of digestion, capacity for exercise and age, together with attention to place and season, before any therapy is chosen.
hinduism.explanation: Ayurvedic treatment is tailored to the individual patient, the state of the disease and the time.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's weighing of patient, disease and season before acting.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close doctrinal match; paraphrased, and the verse reference should be checked against an edition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My son, prove thy soul in thy life, and see what is evil for it, and give not that unto it. For all things are not profitable for all men, neither hath every soul pleasure in every thing.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira teaches that what helps one person may harm another, so each must test what suits him.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's attention to the particular patient rests on the same insight that not everything suits everyone.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; shares individualisation, but is addressed to the self, not to a physician.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that whoever practises medicine without being known for medical knowledge is liable for the harm he causes.
islam.explanation: The hadith makes learning the condition for the right to treat.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise entrusts treatment to katraan, the one who has learned.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified live; supports the learned physician but not the weighing of patient, disease and season.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All of these beneficial habits which we have stated apply only to a healthy man. In contrast, a sick person, or one who has a single organ which is not healthy, or one who has followed a harmful way of life for many years, each of these must choose different patterns of behavior in accordance with his [particular] illness as it is explained in the medical literature.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides insists that the sick must be treated according to their own illness and condition, following the medical books.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's rule that treatment must fit the particular patient and disease as the learned texts direct.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:21 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong fit on individualised treatment; season is treated separately in 4:8 and 4:12.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha distinguishes three kinds of sick people: those who recover whether or not they get suitable food, medicine and nursing, those who do not recover either way, and those who recover only if they get them.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta recognises that different patients respond differently to treatment.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it asks the carer to weigh the particular patient rather than treat all alike.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified live; recognises variation among patients, but its main point is a simile for receptivity to the Dhamma.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Abstinence is briefly of five kinds: with regard to a. substance; b. place; c. time; d. state of mind; e. development.”
jainism.explanation: Jain discipline calibrates even reduced eating by dravya, kshetra, kala and bhava, the substance, place, time and inner state of the one practising it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's weighing of the person, the measure of the illness and the time follows the same habit of judging every practice by its circumstances.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a structural parallel in Jain categories, but it governs ascetic diet, not medical treatment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pindar sings that Asclepius relieved all who came to him, whether with ulcers, wounds, or bodies wasted by summer heat or winter cold, treating some with gentle incantations, some with soothing potions, some with remedies bound on the limbs, and some with the knife.
greek_mythology.explanation: The divine healer chose a different treatment for each sufferer and condition, including those brought on by the season.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Asclepius fits the Kural's learned healer who weighs patient, disease and season before acting.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit, paraphrased: shows treatment varied to the case and season, though without explicit deliberation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...if ten pounds are too much for a particular person to eat and two too little, it does not follow that the trainer will order six pounds; for this also is perhaps too much for the person who is to take it, or too little- too little for Milo, too much for the beginner in athletic exercises.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle's trainer sets the right amount relative to the person, not by a fixed rule.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's physician likewise sets treatment by the measure of the particular patient.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive; strong match on measure relative to the person, without disease or season.

kurals.tamil:
உற்றவன் தீர்ப்பான் மருந்துழைச் செல்வானென்று
அப்பால் நாற்கூற்றே மருந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Utravan theerppaan marundhuzhaich chelvaanendru
appaal naarkootre marundhu.
kurals.meaning: Medicine has four parts: the patient, the physician who cures, the remedy, and the one who stays at hand to prepare and give it.
kurals.elementary: Getting better is like a team game. The sick person must follow the plan, the doctor must know what to do, the medicine must be good, and someone like a parent or nurse must help every day. If one player is missing, the team struggles.
kurals.university: The chapter ends by defining medicine as naarkootru (நாற்கூற்று, 'fourfold'): utravan (உற்றவன், the one afflicted), theerppaan (தீர்ப்பான், the one who cures), marundhu (மருந்து, the remedy), and marundhuzhaich chelvaan (மருந்துழைச் செல்வான், literally 'he who goes near the medicine'). This last term divides the commentators: Varadarasanar reads it as the one who gives the medicine from close by, Kalaignar as the attendant at the bedside, Pappaiah and Kesikan as the preparer or compounder, and Pope's explanation as the compounder. The words appaal (அப்பால், 'that domain') and the closing marundhu frame the whole. Pope's gloss, following Parimelazhagar, adds that each of the four has four qualities in turn, sixteen in all. The fourfold scheme closely matches the Charaka Samhita's 'four feet' of therapy (physician, drug, attendant, patient), which is strong evidence that Valluvar knew the classical medical tradition. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Charaka names the four feet (pada-chatushtaya) of successful treatment as the physician, the drugs, the attendant and the patient, each of which must have its proper qualities.
hinduism.explanation: Classical Ayurveda rests all therapy on these four pillars.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's fourfold medicine, item for item, including the qualities of each that Parimelazhagar's tradition mentions.
hinduism._accuracy_note: A near one-to-one match and likely Valluvar's source tradition; paraphrased because the translation could not be loaded live.

christianity.quote_or_event: “With such doth he heal [men,] and taketh away their pains. Of such doth the apothecary make a confection; and of his works there is no end; and from him is peace over all the earth,”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira describes healing as the joint work of God-given medicines, the physician and the apothecary who compounds them.
christianity.tie_back: The physician, the medicine and the compounder here are three of the Kural's four parts of medicine.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; names physician, medicine and apothecary, though not as a formal fourfold scheme.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet commanded his followers to feed the hungry, visit the sick and set free the captive.
islam.explanation: Visiting and caring for the sick is made a duty for every Muslim, not just for physicians.
islam.tie_back: It honours the Kural's fourth part, the one who stays near the patient.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified live; covers the attendant's role only, not the fourfold scheme.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A Torah Sage is not permitted to live in a community which does not have the following: a doctor, a bloodletter, a bathhouse, a latrine, an available source of water such as a river or a spring, a synagogue, a teacher of children, a scribe, a charity supervisor, a rabbinical court empowered to impose corporal punishment and jail sentences.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides counts a doctor and a medical practitioner among the minimum institutions of a community fit to live in.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats medicine as a structured set of roles that a well-ordered society must provide.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot De'ot 4:23 (tr. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; next-best match, since it lists medical personnel but not the patient-physician-remedy-attendant scheme.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A patient with five qualities is easy to care for. What five? They do what is suitable. They know moderation in what is suitable. They take their medicine. Because their carer wants what's best for them, they accurately report their symptoms by saying when they're getting worse, getting better, or staying the same. And they can endure physical pain...”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the duties of a good patient toward medicine and carer, and in the next sutta the duties of a good carer.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta divides healing into patient, medicine and carer, three of the Kural's four parts, each with its proper qualities.
buddhism.source: Pathama-upatthaka Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 5.123 (tr. Bhikkhu Sujato)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on SuttaCentral; strong fit on the roles and qualities of patient and carer, without the physician as a separate item.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Then the best physicians came to my help, who cure by their medical art and by spells, who were versed in their science, and well knew spells and roots. They tried to cure me according to the fourfold science which they had been taught; but they could not rid me of my pains: hence I say that I am without protection.”
jainism.explanation: The young Anathi recalls that physicians using the fourfold medical science, his father, mother, siblings and devoted wife at his bedside all failed to relieve him, which led him to renounce the world.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain text names the same fourfold medicine as the Kural, then turns it into a lesson that no physician, remedy or attendant can protect the soul from karma.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; Jacobi's note identifies the 'fourfold science' as catuhpada medicine, but the Jain point is its limits, not its sufficiency.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Machaon is wounded, Idomeneus urges Nestor to carry him off, since a physician is worth many other men; later Patroclus sits by the wounded Eurypylus, cuts out the arrow, washes the wound and spreads on it the healing root Achilles learned from Chiron.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer shows both the valued physician and the companion who stays to tend the wounded with the right remedy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Physician, patient, remedy and attending friend, the Kural's four parts, all appear in these scenes.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad 11.514-515 and 11.828-848 (tr. Samuel Butler), paraphrase
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit, paraphrased: all four roles are present but not set out as a scheme.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Life is short, and Art long; the crisis fleeting; experience perilous, and decision difficult. The physician must not only be prepared to do what is right himself, but also to make the patient, the attendants, and externals cooperate.”
philosophy.explanation: The first Hippocratic aphorism says that healing succeeds only when physician, patient, attendants and outward circumstances work together.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's fourfold medicine almost exactly: patient, physician, attendants and the external means of cure.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive; a near one-to-one match, with 'externals' standing for remedies and conditions.
